newsitem.title: UK: City of Moscow debut bond meets high expectations.
newsitem.headline: City of Moscow debut bond meets high expectations.

text.p: The City of Moscow's first international bond launched on Tuesday traded more than 10 basis points tighter amid strong demand immediately after the deal was freed to trade, dealers said.
"People are very bullish on Russia at the moment and they saw a lot of value in this bond," a banker said, adding: "There isn't that much Russian paper out there."
A syndicate manager said: "People were very enthusiastic about this transaction and it's gone extremely well."
The $500 million May 2000 bond was priced to yield 315 basis points over the 6.375 percent May 2000 U.S. Treasury.
The bond traded to around 303 b.p. at 1430 GMT, before some profit-taking took the spread back up to around 307 b.p. The paper is expected to trade between 307-310 b.p, dealers said.
Demand was said to come from a broad spectrum of investors both by area and types of buyers.
"The break-down of investor demand has been fantastic, and it is a clear sign that the roadshow worked extremely well and that Moscow put a lot of work into the deal," a syndicate official said.
Some syndicate officials involved in the deal said the paper was cheaply priced.
"The bond could have been priced more tightly," a syndicate official said.

"All the marketing hype was that Moscow is the superior credit in the region with the bulk of investment and its ratings are constrained by the sovereign so they have paid up for the bond's success," he added.
Moscow is rated Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service and BB- by Standard & Poor's.
Russia's $1.0 billion five-year bond was last trading just inside 300 b.p. over U.S. Treasury notes versus its launch spread of 345 b.p., dealers said.

Some syndicate sources away from the lead said there was speculation of a stipulation from the Russian ministry of finance that the City of Moscow was not able to price itself through where Russia's five-year dollar bond was trading.
But a syndicate manager denied this was the case.
"Investors will take Moscow through where the Federation trades," a dealer said.
Joint lead managers for the transaction Credit Suisse First Boston and Nomura said the size was larger than the $300-$400 million initially mooted due to strong demand.
The bond pays a coupon of 9.50 percent and there is a short first coupon on June 6, 1997.
Chairman of the committee for municipal loans & stock market Mechislav Klimovich recently said Moscow was limited to raise $500 million this year.
